BlogWhy Data Lineage Is Important. # Why Data Lineage Is Important. In the capital markets, any given data point regularly moves through a complex network of operational systems, extract-transform-load (ETL) processes, control and authorization checks, and reporting tools. Data lineage provides the foundation for effective data management, enabling businesses to make informed decisions and drive innovation. As the value of data becomes increasingly prevalent in the capital markets and banks contend with demands to create greater transparency into their business, it’s time to take a closer look at the importance of data lineage. ## What is data lineage? Data lineage is the process that lets a user track, access, and visualize the metadata of information sources, the business logic behind how and why their data is transforming, and the timing associated with a specific data product. ## Use cases where data lineage is critical. * The complexity of preparing data for regulatory reporting often means that firms are stitching together information from multiple systems. ## The challenges of data provenance in legacy systems. Legacy systems — characterized by their age, fragmentation, and outdated architectures — present multiple challenges that inhibit banks from understanding and preserving the provenance of their data. * Legacy processing systems simply don’t track the right level of data lineage. Yet, even with this foresight to record the data, information is often still trapped deep in the system’s internal reports and hard to extract. Because systems were not purpose-built to follow the flow of data, information is commonly not traceable. ## What can your firm do to improve data lineage? What’s more, self-service tools provide managers with data lineage information that enables them to interact with the data programmatically. Modern data platforms play a pivotal role in addressing the challenges banks face when evaluating their legacy systems. By embedding lineage capabilities during the construction of data pipelines, product generation, or reports, businesses ensure a more transparent and traceable data journey. Robust ETL/ELT capabilities will enable you to structure data for multiple use cases and maintain lineage for an auditable trail of information of what transpired and why.

results.title: What Is MES vs ERP vs PLM? | Key Differences Explained
results.content: MES, ERP, and PLM are three key systems used in manufacturing, but they serve different purposes. MES (Manufacturing Execution System) focuses on managing and optimizing the production process on the shop floor. For newly joined engineers, understanding MES is fundamental, as it directly impacts the operational efficiency and quality of manufacturing processes. Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) systems are designed to manage the entire lifecycle of a product from inception, through design and manufacturing, to service and disposal. PLM integrates people, processes, and business systems to provide a product information backbone for companies. While MES, ERP, and PLM systems all play critical roles in manufacturing, they serve distinct purposes and operate at different levels. MES focuses on the shop floor, providing real-time monitoring and control of production processes. It ensures that manufacturing operations are efficient and that products meet quality standards. It manages the development, design, and engineering processes, ensuring that products are brought to market efficiently and meet all necessary standards. While MES and ERP focus on operational and process efficiency, PLM is concerned with product innovation and quality throughout its lifecycle. Despite their distinct roles, MES, ERP, and PLM systems complement each other and can be integrated to provide a comprehensive solution for manufacturing management. MES provides real-time data from the production floor, which can be fed into the ERP system to update inventory levels, production schedules, and financial records. PLM integrates with both MES and ERP to ensure that product designs are accurately translated into manufacturing processes. It provides the necessary data and documentation to MES for production and ensures that ERP systems are updated with the latest product information. In conclusion, MES, ERP, and PLM systems are essential tools for modern manufacturing, each serving a unique purpose within the production process. MES focuses on real-time monitoring and control of manufacturing operations, ensuring efficiency and quality on the shop floor. By integrating MES, ERP, and PLM, manufacturers can achieve greater efficiency, reduce errors, and enhance their overall competitiveness. These systems, when used together, provide a powerful framework for managing the intricate processes of modern manufacturing, ensuring that products are developed, produced, and delivered to the highest standards.

Companies that design, source, and manufacture products often need both PLM (Product Lifecycle Management) and ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning). ## The difference between PLM and ERP. A full function ERP such as Microsoft Dynamics 365 is generally used for the processes that enable the products to be manufactured in the most efficient, cost-controlled manner. ERP solutions handle high volumes of transactional data, so they must be very structured. Often a third-party PLM integrated with Microsoft Dynamics 365 provides the best outcome. Often, not all of a manufacturer’s products are designed in-house, so not everything that goes through the ERP system also requires a PLM system. The products that represent your brand should have started their journey in a PLM application while products that come to you with the design process already completed can go right through to the ERP application, skipping the PLM entirely. For example, let’s say you want to change the style or color of a product in your PLM and then push the new product data through to your ERP. results.title: The Battle for Master Data Supremacy Between PLM, ERP, CRM, MES and Others: Contenders and Approach - Beyond PLM (Product Lifecycle Management) Blog
results.content: The discussion about what is a dominant system in the enterprise has started a long time ago. It was probably true for some time, but already back in the 2000s, the dominance of ERP systems was broken by a strong presence of CRM systems and later by different activities coming from PLM and other domains. While ERP achieved the goal to be ultimate control of all processes starting from finance, the stronghold of ERP as a single source of truth about the product was questioned by many PDM, PLM, and other systems. The idea of data centric approach relies on the capabilities of multiple data management technologies to collect, aggregate and make sense of data that present in multiple systems. Once this repository is built, it can be used for multiple purposes such as data search and navigation, optimizing customer focused tasks in CRM software, concentrating data from many systems in a central ERP system or integrating multiple ERP systems used by a company.
